opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's really one of the open frontiers for us. Right now, a lot of the work in weight space learning, including what we've done with model zoos and hyper-representations, treats the weights in a fairly flat way. You take the parameters, maybe tokenize them layer by layer or into chunks, and you learn a representation over them. That works surprisingly well, but the model doesn't really *understand* that these numbers live inside a particular computational graph.

What I'd like to see is a much tighter coupling between the weights and the structure they sit in. There are a few angles to this. One is symmetries. Neural networks have permutation symmetries, scaling symmetries, and so on, and if your weight space model is blind to those, it wastes a lot of capacity learning that two functionally identical networks are actually the same thing. So building in equivariance, or at least awareness of these symmetries, is one important step, and there's been nice progress from several groups on that.

The second angle is treating the architecture itself as an input, almost like a graph. If you think of a network as nodes and edges, where the weights are attributes on the edges, then you can use graph-based methods that naturally generalize across different widths, depths, even different layer types. That's very appealing because ideally you don't want one generative model per architecture. You want something that, given a description of an architecture, can produce sensible weights for it, much like a language model can produce text in different styles given a prompt.

And then the third piece, which I find really exciting, is going beyond the static structure to the function. Weights only matter because of what the network computes. So if the weight space model can be conditioned on, or trained with signals about, the behavior of the network, like its activations or its performance on data, then it becomes aware not just of the shape of the architecture but of what that architecture is supposed to do.

So in the long run, I'd love to get to a point where you can say: here is an architecture, here's a task, give me a good starting point, or even a fully working set of weights. And for that to work across the zoo of architectures we use in practice, the model really has to internalize architectural structure rather than just memorize flattened parameter vectors.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architectural structure through graph-based methods, but does not propose making the weight-space tokenizer aware of architectural elements.

r002.rationale: It proposes generating weights conditioned on an architecture description, not having the decoder generate architectures conditioned on an architecture signal.

r003.rationale: It does not identify architectures seen in the training collection as the limit of current architecture reconstruction.

r004.rationale: It favors supporting a broad zoo of architectures, but does not specifically connect weight-space learning’s greatest utility to the diversity of open-weight models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's really the crux of where I think the field needs to go. Right now, when we do weight space learning, we mostly treat a trained neural network as a bag of numbers. We flatten the weights, maybe we respect the layer structure a bit, and then we learn representations or even generate new weights from that. But the model doesn't really know what it's looking at. It doesn't know that this tensor is a convolutional kernel that gets slid across an image, or that this one is an attention projection, or that these two matrices are tied together by a residual connection.

And that matters, because weights only have meaning in the context of the computation they're part of. A permutation of neurons in a hidden layer gives you a functionally identical network with completely different raw weights. Scaling one layer up and the next one down gives you the same function again. So if your weight space model isn't aware of those symmetries, it's wasting capacity learning things that don't matter, and it's generalizing poorly across architectures.

So what I'd like to see is weight space learning that takes the computational graph as a first-class input. Think of it as a graph neural network over the architecture itself, where the nodes are neurons or channels and the edges carry the weights, and the message passing respects the actual data flow of the network. There's been nice early work in this direction, with graph-based and equivariant approaches, but I think we're just scratching the surface.

The second thing is conditioning. If I want to generate weights, I should be able to say: here is the architecture, here is the task, here is the data modality, now give me a good initialization or even a fully trained model. Today most of the generative approaches, including some of our own hyper-representation work, are trained on a population of models that share one architecture. That's a real limitation. The exciting version is a single model that has seen many architectures and understands how weights relate to structure, so it can transfer what it learned about a small ResNet to a bigger one, or from vision to a different domain.

And honestly, I think that also opens up the scientific side of this. If the weight space model understands architecture, we can start asking questions like: what do good solutions look like across families of networks, what does the training trajectory reveal about generalization, which parts of the architecture are actually doing the work. That's where weight space learning stops being just a compression or interpolation trick and starts being a way to understand neural networks as objects in their own right.

r001.rationale: The response proposes feeding the computational graph into weight-space learning so the model recognizes architectural elements such as convolutional kernels and attention projections.

r002.rationale: It proposes generating weights conditioned on an architecture signal; it does not propose that the decoder generate architectures.

r003.rationale: It says current approaches often use models sharing one architecture, but does not identify previously encountered architectures as the limit of architecture reconstruction.

r004.rationale: It advocates learning across many architectures and domains, but does not identify diversity among open-weight models as the key utility.

astra-6.text:
I would like to move beyond treating a neural network as just a long vector of weights. Those weights have structure: they belong to particular layers, those layers have different roles, and the connections between them matter. Ideally, a model operating in weight space would understand that structure when it generates weights.

One way to think about it is to condition the generation on a description of the architecture. What are the layers? How are they connected? What shapes do the weight tensors need to have? Then the question becomes whether we can learn something that transfers across architectures, rather than having to learn a separate weight-space model for every architecture.

There’s also the issue that different arrangements of weights can represent the same function. So we want awareness of the architecture without becoming overly sensitive to arbitrary choices, like the ordering of neurons. For me, that combination—respecting the structure while understanding those equivalences—is a really interesting direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses layers, connections, and tensor shapes, but does not propose making a weight-space tokenizer aware of those architectural elements.

r002.rationale: It proposes conditioning weight generation on an architecture description; it does not propose that a decoder generate architectures conditioned on an architecture signal.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify previously encountered training architectures as a limit on architecture reconstruction.

r004.rationale: It mentions transfer across architectures, but does not argue that weight-space learning is most useful when it accommodates the diversity of open-weight models.

sol-6.1.text:
I would like to move beyond treating the weights as just a long vector and actually incorporate the structure of the network. A weight has a particular role: it belongs to a layer, that layer is connected to other layers, and there are symmetries—for example, you can permute neurons without changing the function of the network. Our representation should respect that.

One way to think about this is to represent the architecture as a graph and condition the weight generation on that graph. Then the model can learn both the relationships between weights and the roles they play in the architecture. The exciting question is whether we can transfer what we learn across architectures, rather than having to learn a separate weight space for every network configuration.

r001.rationale: The response says the weight representation should respect network structure, but it does not specifically propose making the weight-space tokenizer aware of architectural elements.

r002.rationale: It proposes conditioning weight generation on an architecture graph, not enabling a decoder to generate architectures from an explicit architecture signal.

r003.rationale: It does not identify previously encountered training architectures as a limit on reconstruction capability.

r004.rationale: It raises transfer across architectures, but does not argue that weight-space learning is most useful when it accommodates diverse open-weight models.
